extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially genre writers: fantasy, science fiction, horror) seeking craft and research advice
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for genre fiction writers on choosing passion-driven topics and doing research so stories are both emotionally engaging and factually convincing. Covers how to find sources, interview experts, and start writing despite perfectionism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write what you want to know
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick something you want to know — what interests you, what moves you emotionally; write about that rather than only writing what you already know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passion for the subject drives deeper research and richer story details (examples: dragons, zombies, monsters). Laurell: “Pick something you want to know. What you’re interested in as a writer.” Howard: passion produces research that grows story elements readers will care about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do your research: books, multiple sources, then experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Start research with books, consult multiple sources, and only then approach experts so you have informed, specific questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell: “First step is books and reading about it... start with books. Then, if you need an expert… talk to an anthropologist or a psychologist.” Emphasizes using authoritative sources before using experts’ time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use encyclopedias/dictionaries with bibliographies as jumping-off points
rubrics_metrics.description: Use reference works (encyclopedias/dictionaries) that provide concise entries and, crucially, strong bibliographies to lead to deeper sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Catherine Briggs’ Dictionary of Fairies as a jumping-off point for folklore research. If a reference lacks a good bibliography, don’t rely on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet as a stepping-off point, not sole research
rubrics_metrics.description: The internet (including Wikipedia) is useful to find keywords and leads, but should not be the only source for factual research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Howard’s method: skim Wikipedia for unfamiliar linked keywords, open those links in new tabs, then follow bibliographies to books and authoritative authors' blogs. Laurell: “You can start with the Internet, it’s a stepping off point, but you also have to make sure it is a book and not someone’s opinion on the Internet.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the Dunning–Kruger effect while researching
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that early, superficial knowledge may make you overconfident; you may be 'too dumb to know how dumb you are' about a subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build foundational knowledge before trusting or using technical details; learn enough basics so you can ask informed questions and avoid catastrophic mistakes (Howard’s driving analogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Research serves two benefits: accuracy and goodwill
rubrics_metrics.description: Thorough research both helps you get technical details right (so knowledgeable readers won’t reject your work) and builds reader goodwill that lets them accept fictional liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dan: “Number one, you’re getting the right stuff right... The other thing is, you are buying goodwill with that research.” Examples: guns, mortuary procedures, or any domain experts might notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use other fiction as primary research
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on other people’s fiction as your main source of factual knowledge about a topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell warns many writers wrongly use fiction as research; fiction can inspire but shouldn’t substitute for factual sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a list of things you love and focus on them
rubrics_metrics.description: As a beginning writer, list the topics and elements you’ve loved since childhood and use those as seeds for projects you’ll sustain and enjoy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell: make a list of the things that interest you; these durable loves help you stay engaged (example: childhood fascination with monster movies leading to a career writing monsters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Give yourself enough ‘toys’ — keep writing fun to sustain long projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a variety of elements that interest you in your work so the act of writing remains enjoyable over many books or a long series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell: if she’d written a straight mystery she wouldn’t have kept interest for 20+ books; adding fantastic elements keeps her having fun. Framing writing as play increases longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask experts focused, informed questions; respect their time
rubrics_metrics.description: When you contact practitioners or scholars, come prepared with specific questions framed after your book-based research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell: “Don’t just go to somebody and say, ‘Tell me everything you know about X or Y.’ You need good questions, because you don’t want to waste their time.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Research can generate new story ideas beyond factual accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Research often yields unexpected details or perspectives that inspire fresh plot elements, worldbuilding, and character beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell’s voodoo research produced new ideas (even while noting real voodoo lacks shambling dead); audience members appreciated that she’d done real research, and it informed creative choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start writing now — use prompts and ‘just get started’ to overcome paralysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t wait for perfect knowledge; begin writing from any sentence or prompt to discover whether you have a story and to produce material to revise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell’s fish-head metaphor: chop off the fish head by writing the beginning — e.g. prompt: “I was walking home from work one day.” Starting produces the material you can shape later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use effective quick-research strategies to learn enough to proceed
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt practical methods (skimming, following linked keywords, finding authoritative authors/blogs) to build working knowledge efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Howard’s workflow: skim Wikipedia for unfamiliar linked terms, open linked pages to build vocabulary, then follow bibliographies to books or authors’ blogs; accepts that this can be time-consuming but effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-check sources; don’t rely on a single account
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate facts across multiple reputable sources to avoid basing your work on a single, potentially incorrect account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell: “Take multiple sources.” If a source lacks corroboration or a bibliography, be skeptical.
